Covered per-token pricing assumptions, batching and cache leverage, VPC requirements, and pilot scope. Next steps: send cost model, schedule deeper technical session, share security artifacts.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Jordan from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Ethan: Ethan here, I'm CTO at Slate.
[00:10] Priya: Priya - Head of ML.
[00:12] Liam: Liam, SRE.
[00:15] Amira: Amira, product.
[00:20] Maya (SE): Maya from Redwood on the technical side.
[00:28] Jordan: Great. Objective for today's call is to understand workload shape and budget constraints so we can recommend hosted, dedicated, or private. We'll talk per-token assumptions and levers like batching and caching that move the needle.
[01:02] Ethan: High level — we run a customer support assistant and docs summarizer. Volume is spiky: 2k qpd normal, bursts to 50k during campaigns. Latency target ~250-500ms for short chat, longer for batch summaries is okay.
[01:22] Priya: Also want data residency — some logs must stay in our VPC.
[01:28] Jordan: Got it. Quick question on sequence lengths?
[01:32] Priya: Median context ~512 tokens, mean maybe 700, 95th at 4k for some long doc queries.
[01:40] Maya: That's helpful. For economics, those longer tails matter a lot because cost scales with generation tokens and KV cache memory.
[01:55] Ethan: Walk us through the per-token math — hosted versus dedicated.
[02:00] Jordan: Sure. Hosted is OPEX, you pay per token with tiered pricing; good if you want fast setup and variable load. Dedicated is reserved capacity — predictable cost, better for steady high volume where unit cost drops. Private has higher fixed cost but gives control for residency and auditability.
[02:28] Maya: Some specific levers: batching, auto-prefix/KV caching, and quantization profiles. Batching improves GPU utilization — if you can tolerate 50-100ms extra queuing, unit cost can drop 20-60% depending on mix.
[02:48] Liam: For us, queueing is risky during campaigns. We need predictable P95 latency.
[02:54] Priya: Correct, we can't have 200-300ms jitter spikes.
[02:58] Jordan: We can set routing policies: route mission-critical low-latency traffic to dedicated or lower batch pools, and route non-critical bulk summaries to higher-batch cheaper pools. That’s a common pattern.
[03:18] Ethan: What about caching — you said KV cache. How does that reduce cost?
[03:22] Maya: KV/prefix cache keeps model key-value states for repeated contexts so for chat-like flows each turn after the first can be served with fewer compute ops — effectively reduces repeated forward passes. For certain flows you can see 30-70% token equivalent savings. But it's workload dependent.
[03:45] Priya: Any drawbacks? Complexity?
[03:48] Maya: Mainly memory footprint and eviction policy tuning. Also, for private deployments the cache lives in their infra which changes ops.
[03:58] Jordan: Important to note our hosted keeps KV encrypted and we support optional customer-managed keys via KMS for enterprise tiers.
[04:08] Amira: Ok on compliance we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs. Do you have those?
[04:12] Jordan: Yes — SOC2, SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs are in our docs. We'll send the pack.
[04:20] Ethan: Back to numbers — can you give a sample per-token comparison with their numbers?
[04:26] Maya: If we assume 700 tokens per request and 2k qpd baseline, that's ~1.4M tokens/day. With hosted list price at X (we'll put actual numbers in the spreadsheet), you can run hosted with burst credits, but per-token cost may be 1.0-1.4x higher than dedicated. If you reserve capacity and tune batching aggressively, dedicated can be 30-50% cheaper at scale.
[04:54] Priya: For bursts to 50k, how does dedicated handle that?
[04:58] Jordan: Dedicated can have burst pools or autoscale rules. We recommend a small reserved baseline for predictable traffic and allow short-lived burst capacity; there's also a graceful fallback to compatible smaller model variants to preserve SLOs.
[05:15] Ethan: How do you price bursts? Is that additional over the commit?
[05:18] Jordan: Bursts are billed at overage rates unless you buy burst credits or a higher tier. We'll model that in the spreadsheet.
[05:26] Liam: Latency: you mentioned kernel selection and compilation — how much variance is there across sequence lengths?
[05:30] Maya: We pick kernels optimized for expected sequence length distribution. Longer sequences cost more per token because attention is O(n^2) in some layers, but optimized kernels and quantization reduce absolute cost. We can quantify expected P50/P95 latencies in the deep-dive.
[05:50] Priya: Quantization — do you support int8 or 4-bit? Any hallucination/regression risks?
[05:56] Maya: We support quantization-friendly execution paths and recommend testing for quality regressions. For many models, int8 gives minimal quality drop; 4-bit may need evals. Our Optimize team provides quantization recommendations per workload.
[06:12] Jordan: On pilot scope — common approach: 4-week pilot on hosted with sample traffic, measure real token mix, then switch to dedicated if cost-op favorable. Alternative is a short private proof-of-concept in customer VPC.
[06:28] Ethan: We prefer private for data locality, but cost/time to stand up worries me. How long does private take?
[06:34] Maya: Private deployment typically 4-8 weeks including network setup, KMS, and on-prem packaging if needed. Hosted can be immediate. Dedicated sits in the middle — a couple of weeks for capacity reservation and routing setup.
[06:52] Amira: Success criteria for us would be unit cost under $0.00X per generated token? (laughter)
[06:59] Jordan: We'll put realistic dollars in the model.
[07:02] Priya: Can you show sample plan with 95th percentile tails included? That's the part that kills our budget.
[07:08] Maya: Absolutely — send your P50/P95 distribution and we'll show sensitivity: if your P95 moves from 1k to 4k tokens, cost could rise 2-3x unless you use caching and routing to dedicated pools for the heavy tails.
[07:25] Ethan: Any suggestions for pre-token reduction like truncation or prompt engineering?
[07:29] Priya: We are already doing chunking and retrieval augmentation. But some queries still need full docs.
[07:33] Maya: We typically recommend hybrid: aggressive retrieval for first-pass, then on-demand full-doc summaries for cases flagged as high-value. That shrinks average context and preserves quality for important queries.
[07:48] Jordan: Question from our side: what stakeholders will sign off on a pilot?
[07:52] Ethan: Exec sponsor is me, Priya owns ML validation, Liam owns infra sign-off. Amira will own product metrics.
[07:59] Jordan: Great. Another technical note — data retention: hosted allows configurable retention windows, but if you need zero retention we recommend private with customer-managed KMS.
[08:12] Amira: We need logs retained for six months for audits.
[08:16] Jordan: That is supported; retention tiers may affect cost.
[08:20] Liam: Networking — for hosted, can you do VPC peering or private link?
[08:24] Maya: Yes, we support PrivateLink and customer VPC peering for enterprise tiers. We'll include network diagram examples.
[08:30] Ethan: Any hidden fees — egress, storage for KV caches?
[08:34] Jordan: Egress can apply for cross-region traffic. KV cache memory is included in dedicated pricing but in private we size per-customer and that affects cost. We'll surface all these line items.
[08:48] Priya: For benchmarking, what artifacts do you need from us?
[08:52] Maya: Ideally: representative prompt set, token length distribution, QPS over time, and a few sample request/response logs (sanitized). Also we need target latency SLOs per route.
[09:05] Ethan: We'll sanitize and send.
[09:08] Jordan: Pricing model — we'll send a sheet with three scenarios: hosted baseline, dedicated reserve for steady state plus burst costs, and private TCO with infra amortized over 1-2 years. We'll also include sensitivity to batching and caching.
[09:24] Amira: How do you measure the impact of caching and batching in the model?
[09:28] Maya: We simulate hit rates for prefix/KV cache and different batch sizes. For example, at 30% cache hit rate and 8-16 request batch sizes for summaries, you can expect ~35% unit cost reduction. But if you require strict P95 latency the allowable batch window shrinks and savings drop.
[09:51] Priya: What's the typical batch wait we can allow? 50ms? 100ms?
[09:55] Maya: Many customers accept <100ms queuing on non-critical routes. For chat low-latency we aim for <20-30ms queuing. It's configurable per route.
[10:07] Ethan: Any examples where customers moved from hosted to dedicated and saw X?
[10:10] Jordan: Yes — one marketplace customer scaled to 10M tokens/day; switched to dedicated and saw 40% unit cost reduction after enabling batching and a quantization profile. We'll anonymize the case study and send it.
[10:22] Liam: On SLA — what do you offer for dedicated?
[10:26] Jordan: Dedicated comes with an uptime SLA and latency targets; exact numbers depend on commitment level. We'll include the SLA matrix.
[10:34] Priya: For evaluation, we want to run a 2-week pilot capturing real traffic. Can we do hosted pilot with VPC peering and customer-managed keys?
[10:41] Maya: Hosted enterprise tier supports VPC peering + CMK for encryption. That can be used for a hosted pilot that approximates data locality.
[10:50] Ethan: Useful. Let's talk timelines: we want pilot in Feb. Is that feasible?
[10:55] Jordan: Yes — hosted pilot can be started in days once we have access and sample prompts. Dedicated pilot provisioning might take 1-2 weeks. Private is longer.
[11:06] Amira: Any blockers from our side?
[11:08] Liam: We need legal review and procurement timelines; also security will want the SOC2 artifacts.
[11:12] Jordan: We'll send the security pack and the SOW template.
[11:16] Priya: On cost — can you provide per-month estimated ranges?
[11:19] Jordan: We'll include ranges in the sheet across low/median/high traffic and include unit costs with and without batching+cache.
[11:27] Maya: Quick note — for 95th tail savings we often recommend routing heavy-doc queries to an offline summary pipeline instead of the LLM where possible; that changes product UX but can drastically cut token spend.
[11:40] Ethan: Good idea. We'll evaluate.
[11:44] Jordan: Wrapping up — agree to next steps: Jordan to send cost model and security artifacts; Maya to prepare throughput estimate and run a quick sim; slate team to send prompt distribution and sanitized logs.
[11:58] Amira: Thanks everyone.
[12:00] Ethan: Thanks — looking forward.
[12:05] Jordan: We'll follow up with scheduling the deep-dive.
[12:09] Maya: Thanks all, bye.
